title: BST with three traversals
statement:
Mohan keeps the employee IDs of his company in a binary search tree, where the IDs smaller than the ID of a node are placed in its left subtree, and the other IDs are placed in its right subtree. The function insert adds a new ID to the tree. The program prints the three traversals of the tree: the preorder traversal visits the node, then its left subtree, and then its right subtree; the inorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, and then the right subtree; and the postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, and then the node.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (IDs in the order added).
Output Format: "Preorder:", "Inorder:", "Postorder:" lines, each value preceded by a space.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20; 1 <= ID <= 1000; all IDs different.
easy: Insert IDs into a BST, then print all three depth-first traversals. Inorder of a BST is always sorted - use it to sanity-check.
logic: insert: empty -> new node; value < data -> left; else -> right (recursive).
preorder = root, left, right. inorder = left, root, right. postorder = left, right, root.
Each print helper writes "Label:" first, then " value" per node, then endl.
algorithm: Node* insert(Node* root, int value): standard recursive BST insert.
void preorder(Node* root): if NULL return; print " " + data; recurse left; recurse right.
void inorder: recurse left; print; recurse right. void postorder: recurse left; recurse right; print.
main: read n, insert all, call the three print helpers.
mistakes: Mixing the visit order of preorder and postorder (root FIRST vs root LAST).
Printing values with a trailing space - use " " before each value.
Forgetting the NULL base case -> crash.

title: BST search, minimum and maximum
statement:
Nirmala is a librarian who stores the book numbers of her library in a binary search tree. The function searchResult returns the message "Found" if a given book number is present in the tree, or "Not Found" otherwise. The function findMin returns the smallest book number in the tree, and the function findMax returns the largest book number in the tree.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers. Line 3: integer key.
Output Format: "Search: " + Found/Not Found; "Minimum: " + smallest; "Maximum: " + largest.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20; 1 <= book number, key <= 1000; all book numbers different.
easy: Search by walking left/right; minimum = keep going LEFT; maximum = keep going RIGHT.
logic: searchResult loops while temp != NULL comparing key with data.
findMin walks temp = temp->left until the left child is NULL.
findMax walks temp = temp->right until the right child is NULL.
algorithm: string searchResult(Node* root, int key): while temp: if equal return "Found"; else temp = (key < data) ? left : right; return "Not Found".
int findMin(Node* root): while (temp->left != NULL) temp = temp->left; return temp->data.
int findMax(Node* root): while (temp->right != NULL) temp = temp->right; return temp->data.
main: build BST, read key, print the three lines.
mistakes: Walking the wrong direction in findMin/findMax (left gives the MINIMUM, not the maximum).
Searching recursively without a base case -> crash on missing keys.
QB source note: sample 1's input is printed without the leading n line; n = 5 is reconstructed from the input format.

title: AVL single rotation at the root
statement:
Pavithra stores the roll numbers of a class in a binary search tree. The height of an empty tree is 0. The balance factor of a node is the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. If the balance factor of the root is greater than 1, the tree is rebalanced with a single right rotation at the root. If the balance factor of the root is less than -1, the tree is rebalanced with a single left rotation at the root. Otherwise, the tree is not changed. The function rebalance does this, and the program prints the preorder traversal of the tree after it is rebalanced.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (roll numbers in insertion order).
Output Format: "Preorder After Balancing:" + preorder of the (possibly rotated) tree.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20; all roll numbers different; a single rotation always suffices.
easy: Insert keys into a plain BST, compute the root's balance factor, and apply one right or left rotation if the root is unbalanced.
logic: height(empty) = 0; height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)).
balanceFactor = height(left) - height(right).
bf > 1 -> rotateRight(root): x = root->left; root->left = x->right; x->right = root; return x.
bf < -1 -> rotateLeft symmetric. Otherwise the tree stays.
algorithm: int height(Node* root): 0 for NULL; else 1 + max of children heights.
int balanceFactor(Node* root): height(left) - height(right).
Node* rotateRight(Node* y) and Node* rotateLeft(Node* x) as above.
Node* rebalance(Node* root): apply the matching rotation or return root unchanged.
main: build BST, rebalance, print preorder.
mistakes: Forgetting to RETURN the new subtree root after a rotation - the caller must receive x, not the old root.
Using node-count heights and edge-count heights inconsistently (pick one; the QB solution counts nodes: empty = 0).
Rebalancing every node instead of only the root (the task limits rotation to the root).
note: 40 30 20 10 -> left chain, right rotation gives preorder 30 20 10 40.

title: Expression tree: build from postfix, print infix and evaluate
statement:
Rajesh builds a calculator that stores an arithmetic expression as an expression tree. In an expression tree, every leaf is an operand and every other node is an operator whose left subtree and right subtree are its two operands. The tree is built from a postfix expression, where the operator comes after its two operands. Every operand is a single digit, and the operators are +, -, *, and /, where / is an integer division. The function printInfix prints the expression in the infix form with a pair of brackets around every operator and its operands, and the function evaluate returns the value of the expression.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: One line: string expr (valid postfix of digits and + - * /).
Output Format: Line 1: "Infix: " + bracketed infix. Line 2: "Value: " + integer value.
Constraints: 3 <= length of expr <= 49; no division by zero.
easy: Build the tree with a node stack (same as Unit 3), then print it with brackets and evaluate it recursively.
logic: build: operand -> leaf pushed; operator -> pop right, pop left, attach, push the operator node.
infix print: leaf -> digit; else '(' + left + operator + right + ')'.
evaluate: leaf -> data - '0'; else apply the operator to the two recursive results.
Integer division for '/'.
algorithm: Node* build(string postfix): stack of Node*; loop chars; return the final stack top.
void infix(Node* root): recursive bracketed print.
int evaluate(Node* root): recursive evaluation with + - * and integer /.
main: read expr; root = build(expr); printInfix(root); print "Value: " << evaluate(root).
mistakes: Popping left before right (mirrors - and / subtrees).
Printing digits with brackets - leaves print bare.
Character arithmetic: data - '0' converts '8' to 8; forgetting it gives ASCII values.
note: Source anomaly: sample 2's input shows only '+' while its output is (9+(5-1)) / 13 - the only postfix input matching that output is 951-+, so the input was reconstructed.

title: Trie with insert and whole-word search
statement:
Sridevi builds a spelling checker that stores the words of a dictionary in a trie. Every node of the trie has 26 links, one for each lowercase letter, and a flag that tells whether a word ends at that node. The function insert adds a word to the trie, and the function search returns "Found" only if the whole word is present in the trie as a word that was inserted, and "Not Found" otherwise. A word that is only a prefix of an inserted word, but was not inserted itself, is not found.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n strings (dictionary). Line 3: integer q. Line 4: q strings (queries).
Output Format: q lines: word + ": " + Found/Not Found.
Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 50; 1 <= word length <= 20; lowercase letters only.
easy: Store words letter by letter in a trie; a query is Found only if every letter has a path AND the last node's end flag is true.
logic: insert walks/creates the children for each letter and sets isEnd = true at the end.
search walks the children; a missing child -> "Not Found"; after the walk, isEnd decides.
A prefix like 'ea' in 'ear' walks fine but isEnd is false -> "Not Found".
algorithm: TrieNode* createNode(): 26 NULL children, isEnd = false.
void insert(string word): temp = root; for each letter: index = letter - 'a'; create child if missing; temp = child; set temp->isEnd = true.
string search(string word): walk; if a child is missing return "Not Found"; return isEnd ? "Found" : "Not Found".
main: insert all dictionary words, then answer each query word + ": " + result.
mistakes: Returning "Found" when the walk succeeds but isEnd is false (prefix-only match).
Indexing children without letter - 'a' (using the raw character as an index).
Forgetting to set isEnd at the end of insert.
note: QB source note: sample 2's input lacks its leading count line; n = 2 is reconstructed from the input format.

title: Family tree: nodes, leaves, height, full check
statement:
Lakshman is a genealogist who studies a family tree in which every person has at most two children. The people are numbered from 0 to n-1, and the person 0 is the oldest ancestor, who is the root of the tree. For every person, the number of the left child and the number of the right child are given, and -1 means that the child does not exist. Write a program that prints the number of people, the number of people who have no children (the leaves), and the height of the tree. The height of the tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf, so a tree with only the root has height 0. Also print whether the tree is a full binary tree, which means that every person has either no child or exactly two children.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Next n lines: two integers l, r (left and right child of person i).
Output Format: "Nodes: ", "Leaves: ", "Height: " lines and "Full Binary Tree: Yes/No".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50; -1 <= l, r < n; data always forms a valid tree rooted at 0.
easy: Read each person's children into arrays, then count leaves (both children -1), compute height in edges recursively, and check the full rule (0 or 2 children, never exactly 1).
logic: height(node): -1 for a missing child; else 1 + max(height(l), height(r)) -> root height counts edges.
Leaf: left == -1 AND right == -1.
Full violation: exactly ONE child exists (left XOR right).
algorithm: Read n and all (l, r) pairs into leftChild[] and rightChild[].
Count leaves in a loop.
full = true; if a node has exactly one child, full = false.
height(0) with the -1-for-empty convention.
Print the four lines.
mistakes: Returning 0 for a missing child in height - it must be -1 so that a leaf gets height 0 (edges).
Marking a node with one child as full - it is NOT (sample 2: node 1 has only a right child -> No).
Counting the root when n = 1: Nodes 1, Leaves 1, Height 0, Full: Yes.

title: Red-black colouring validator with black height
statement:
Dr. Subramanian teaches data structures and checks the colouring of the trees drawn by his students. Every node of a tree is coloured either red (R) or black (B). The tree is a correct red-black tree colouring if it follows all these rules: the root is black; a red node never has a red child; and every path from the root down to an empty link has the same number of black nodes. The empty links are not counted as nodes. The number of black nodes on such a path is called the black height of the tree. The ordering of the keys is already correct, and it does not have to be checked. Write a program that reads a coloured binary tree and prints whether it is a correct red-black tree colouring, and the black height of the tree if it is correct.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Next n lines: key, color (R/B), left child, right child (-1 = none). Node 0 is the root.
Output Format: "Valid Red-Black Tree" + "Black Height: <h>" or "Invalid Red-Black Tree".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50; 1 <= key <= 1000; -1 <= l, r < n.
easy: Check the three rules with one recursive function that returns the black height, or -1 as soon as any rule fails.
logic: Root must be black - check before recursing.
blackHeight(node): 0 for an empty link; a red node with a red child -> -1; recurse both sides; if either is -1 or they differ -> -1; a black node adds 1 to the common value.
-1 propagates all the way up as 'invalid'.
algorithm: Read nodes into arrays color[], leftChild[], rightChild[].
If color[0] == 'R' -> print Invalid and stop.
bh = blackHeight(0); if bh == -1 -> Invalid; else print Valid and "Black Height: " + bh.
blackHeight(int node): if node == -1 return 0; check red-red with both children; l = bh(left); r = bh(right); validate; return l + (color == 'B' ? 1 : 0).
mistakes: Counting empty links as black nodes - they contribute 0.
Adding 1 for red nodes (only BLACK nodes increase the black height).
Checking red-red only on the left child and forgetting the right child.
note: Sample 2 (two black nodes in a chain) fails the equal-black-count rule -> Invalid.

title: Trie prefix counter (autocomplete suggestions)
statement:
Uma is a developer of a search box that suggests words while a user is typing. A dictionary of words is given, and for every prefix that the user types, the search box must show how many words of the dictionary start with that prefix. A word also starts with itself, so a word that is equal to the prefix is counted too. Write a program that stores the dictionary in a trie, where every node keeps the number of the words that pass through it, and prints the number of words for every prefix typed by the user.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n strings. Line 3: integer q. Line 4: q strings (prefixes).
Output Format: q lines: prefix + ": " + count.
Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 50; 1 <= length <= 20; lowercase only; all dictionary words different.
easy: While inserting each word, add +1 to every node it passes through; a prefix query then just reads the counter at the end of its path (0 if the path breaks).
logic: Every node has children[26] and int count.
Insert: walk/create children; after moving into a child, child->count++.
Query: walk; missing child -> answer 0; else answer temp->count.
algorithm: createNode(): 26 NULL children, count = 0.
Insert each dictionary word updating counts on the way down.
For each prefix: walk from the root; if a child is missing, result = 0; otherwise result = temp->count.
Print prefix + ": " + result.
mistakes: Incrementing count BEFORE moving into the child (counts on the wrong node).
Printing 0 incorrectly when the prefix path exists but... no: if the path exists the counter is already correct; 0 happens only when the path breaks.
Using isEnd flags and counting words at the end instead of pass-through counts (does not answer prefix queries).

title: AVL imbalance diagnosis: balance factor and rotation type
statement:
Ms. Kalpana teaches AVL trees and wants to tell her students which rotation is needed at the root of a tree. The keys are added one by one, in the given order, to an empty binary search tree, where the keys smaller than the key of a node go to its left subtree, and the other keys go to its right subtree. No rotation is done while the keys are added. The height of an empty tree is 0, and the balance factor of a node is the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. If the balance factor of the root is between -1 and 1, no rotation is needed. Otherwise, the rotation is decided by the balance factor of the taller child of the root: root BF > 1 and left child BF >= 0: LL (single right rotation); root BF > 1 and left child BF < 0: LR (double rotation, left and then right); root BF < -1 and right child BF <= 0: RR (single left rotation); root BF < -1 and right child BF > 0: RL (double rotation, right and then left). Write a program that prints the balance factor of the root and the rotation needed.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (keys in insertion order).
Output Format: "Balance Factor: " + bf; "Rotation: " + LL/LR/RR/RL/None.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20; all keys different.
easy: Build the plain BST with arrays (no rotation), compute the root's balance factor and the taller child's factor, then name the case.
logic: Insert every key into a leftChild/rightChild array BST.
height(node) counts NODES (empty = 0, leaf = 1) exactly as the problem statement says (empty tree height 0).
bf = height(left) - height(right) at the root.
bf > 1: left child is taller -> its bf >= 0 means LL else LR. bf < -1: right child bf <= 0 means RR else RL. Else None.
algorithm: Read keys; insert each into the array-based BST.
int height(int node): 0 for -1; else 1 + max(height(l), height(r)).
int balance(int node): height(l) - height(r).
bf = balance(0); print it.
Apply the four-case decision table and print LL / LR / RR / RL / None.
mistakes: Mixing edge-heights and node-heights - the statement fixes empty = 0 and the leaf contributes height 1.
Choosing LR when the LEFT child leans LEFT (that is LL) - always check the CHILD's balance factor.
Inserting equal keys - all keys are distinct by constraint.
